title: What is a North Star Metric? Definition and Selection
meta_description: A north star metric is the single number a team steers by. How to pick one, the tests it has to pass, and the reported figures that fail every one of them.
h1: What is a north star metric?
primary_keyword: what is a north star metric
secondary_keywords: how to choose a north star metric

visuals.alt: Six reference points for choosing a north star metric: the share of companies that track activation, the share of users who never reach first value, the top-decile against median activation gap, the standing LTV to CAC bar, platform-reported against true return on ad spend, and the SaaS-only activation median, each row carrying its source and verification date
visuals.caption: What a north star candidate has to survive. Verified 30 September 2026.

faq.q: What makes a good north star metric?
faq.a: It has to move before revenue does, respond to work the team controls, and break if the product gets worse. A metric that only rises is a vanity metric with a plan attached.

faq.q: Should revenue be the north star metric?
faq.a: Rarely. Revenue is the outcome, and it lags too far behind the work to steer by. The better candidate is the leading indicator that predicts it, which for most product-led companies is activation.

faq.q: How many north star metrics should a team have?
faq.a: One, with a small set of inputs beneath it. Aggregating independently-set team goals produces a list, and a list is a tracker rather than a direction.

unique_value_statement: Gives three falsifiable tests a candidate metric has to pass and then applies them to a real reported figure that fails — platform-reported return on ad spend against true return after commission — instead of listing well-known companies' metrics.
